correctness.rationale: For fixed q>=2, count each palindrome-prefix/suffix split s to get at most (m+1)q^(ceil(m/2)+1) admissible length-m targets. At odd m, each of m cyclic-reflection cut classes has exactly q^((m+1)/2) words. A primitive word cannot occur under two distinct reflections, since their composition is a nonidentity rotation; at most m q^(m/3) words are nonprimitive, as any proper period divisor of odd m is <=m/3. Hence |P_{q,m}|>=m(q^((m+1)/2)-m q^(m/3))=Omega_q(m q^(m+1)/2) for sufficiently large odd m. For any target w, X counts its M=N-m+1 possible starts. Overlapping simultaneous hits at shift d<m have probability <=q^(-m-d), and nonoverlapping hits are independent; E X^2 <= mu^2+mu(1+2/(q-1)), mu=M q^-m. Paley-Zygmund/Cauchy-Schwarz yields P(X>0)>=mu/(mu+1+2/(q-1)), with union upper bound min(1,Nq^-m). Summing target counts above/below h=floor(log_q N) gives O_q(sqrt N log_q N), and choosing the largest odd m<=h gives matching Omega, covering all large N and both parities of h. A newly written direct checker (not imported from repository) enumerated q=2 odd m=3,5,7,9,11 and q=3 odd m=3,5,7,9, plus exact q=2,N=4..7 and q=3,N=4..6 random-host expectations and occurrence inequalities. These finite tests corroborate, but do not substitute for, the general proof. No substantive correctness gap found.

value.rationale: The quantity is a natural extension of palindromic richness: count distinct contiguous factors of a random word that have palindromic length at most two. The result identifies a genuine log N increase over the known Theta(sqrt N) behavior of single palindromes. The explanation is structural: odd-length primitive necklace/reflection cuts contribute a linear-in-m multiplicity of allowable words, and overlapping-hit control translates this to realized random-host distinctness. It holds for every fixed alphabet q>=2 rather than an arbitrary tiny slice. It is an order theorem, not a sharp coefficient, and its straightforward second-moment methods limit depth, but the unknown exact natural growth order is a useful standalone fact beyond reprinting the Kemp census.
